\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}
Bucketed lookup is the workhorse of practical data structures. One fixes a map from a
key universe into a set of bucket labels; keys landing in the same bucket collide and
are resolved by a linear scan. The classical analysis is probabilistic and asymptotic:
assume the bucket map behaves like a random function, conclude that the expected chain
length is $O(N/m)$, and stop.

This paper takes the opposite stance. We fix no randomness, make no distributional
assumption on the keys, and prove statements that are \emph{exact}: identities where
an identity is available, and inequalities that are attained, with the attaining
objects identified. The result is a complete description---floor, ceiling, optimal
locus, symmetry group, and trade-off constant---of the deterministic combinatorics
underlying bucketed lookup.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
\item A precise formulation of what it means for the cost model to be \emph{honest}:
the scan code (bucket label, intra-bucket index) is a uniquely decodable code
(Theorems~\ref{thm:honest} and \ref{thm:unique}).
\item An exact accounting identity converting total decoding cost into a sum of
triangular numbers of bucket sizes (Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting}).
\item The exact pigeonhole optimum with its attaining scheme
(Theorems~\ref{thm:lower} and \ref{thm:optimum}), via an integral tangent-line
inequality (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent}).
\item Rigidity: the optimal locus is exactly the set of balanced profiles
(Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity}), with symmetry invariance
(Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetry}) identifying it as a single orbit.
\item Perfect hashing characterised, and a pigeonhole failure analysis
(Theorems~\ref{thm:perfect} and \ref{thm:failure}).
\item The exact maximum $T(N)$ and the cost window
(Theorems~\ref{thm:max} and \ref{thm:window}), with the exact description of the
achievable set (Proposition~\ref{prop:achievable}) showing the window is porous.
\item The mean-cost bound and the $\varepsilon$-compression barrier with a matching
equality case (Theorems~\ref{thm:mean}, \ref{thm:barrier}, \ref{thm:sharp}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Notation}
Throughout, $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$; $A$ denotes a finite totally ordered set of
\emph{keys} with $|A| = N$, and $B$ a finite set of \emph{bucket labels} with $|B| = m$.
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ write
\[
T(k) = \frac{k(k+1)}{2} = 1 + 2 + \cdots + k
\]
for the $k$-th triangular number, and set $q = \lfloor N/m\rfloor$, $r = N \bmod m$
whenever $m \ge 1$, so $N = mq + r$ with $0 \le r < m$.

\section{The model}

\begin{definition}[Scan scheme]
A \emph{scan scheme} on keys $A$ with bucket labels $B$ is a function $b_S : A \to B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fibre, scan list]
For $\ell \in B$, the \emph{fibre} is $F_S(\ell) = \{x \in A : b_S(x) = \ell\}$, and the
\emph{scan list} $L_S(\ell)$ is the list of elements of $F_S(\ell)$ in increasing
order. It is duplicate-free of length $|F_S(\ell)|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Intra-bucket index, decoding cost]
The \emph{intra-bucket index} of a key $x$ is $i_S(x)$, the $0$-based position of $x$ in
$L_S(b_S(x))$; the \emph{decoding cost} is $\cost_S(x) = i_S(x) + 1$, the $1$-based
number of comparisons a linear scan of $x$'s bucket performs before locating $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Scan code]
The \emph{scan code} of $x$ is $\enc_S(x) = \bigl(b_S(x), i_S(x)\bigr) \in B \times
\mathbb{N}$, and the partial decoding map $\dec_S$ sends $(\ell,i)$ to the $i$-th entry
of $L_S(\ell)$ if $i < |F_S(\ell)|$, and to $\bot$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Total and mean cost]
The \emph{total decoding cost} is $C(S) = \sum_{x \in A} \cost_S(x)$; the \emph{mean
decoding cost} is $C(S)/N$.
\end{definition}

Two design choices deserve comment. Using the canonical increasing order inside each
bucket is not a restriction: a scan of a bucket of size $k$ retrieves its $k$ keys at
costs $1,2,\dots,k$ in some order, whatever the order chosen, so the total is
unaffected. And costing a lookup by comparisons is the standard atomic model; all
statements below scale linearly under a change of unit.

\section{Honesty of the model}

\begin{theorem}[Honest decoding]\label{thm:honest}
For every scan scheme $S$ and every key $x$, $\dec_S\bigl(\enc_S(x)\bigr) = x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By construction $x \in F_S(b_S(x))$, so $x$ occurs in $L_S(b_S(x))$. For any list, the
entry at the position of the first occurrence of an element is that element, and
$i_S(x)$ is exactly that position.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of decoding]\label{thm:unique}
For every scan scheme $S$, every $(\ell,i) \in B \times \mathbb{N}$ and every key $x$,
\[
\dec_S(\ell,i) = x \iff (\ell,i) = \enc_S(x).
\]
Consequently $\enc_S$ is injective: the scan code is a uniquely decodable code.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) is Theorem~\ref{thm:honest}. For ($\Rightarrow$), if $\dec_S(\ell,i)=x$
then $x$ occurs in $L_S(\ell)$, so $b_S(x)=\ell$, and $i$ is a legal index with
$L_S(\ell)[i]=x$. As $L_S(\ell)$ is duplicate-free, the position of an element is
determined by the element, so $i = i_S(x)$. Injectivity follows by applying $\dec_S$ to
an equality of codes.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Index range]\label{cor:range}
$i_S(x) < |F_S(b_S(x))|$, hence $1 \le \cost_S(x) \le |F_S(b_S(x))|$.
\end{corollary}

Restricted to a single bucket, Theorem~\ref{thm:unique} says $i_S$ is injective on
$F_S(\ell)$: no two keys of a bucket share an index.

\begin{lemma}[List cost]\label{lem:listcost}
For every duplicate-free list $L$ of length $k$,
$\sum_{x \in L}\bigl(\pos_L(x) + 1\bigr) = T(k)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $L$. For $L = a :: L'$ with $a \notin L'$, the head contributes $1$ and
each $x \in L'$ satisfies $\pos_L(x) = \pos_{L'}(x)+1$, so the tail contributes
$T(k-1) + (k-1)$. The total is $T(k-1)+k = T(k)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cost accounting]\label{thm:accounting}
For every scan scheme $S$,
\[
C(S) \;=\; \sum_{x \in A} \cost_S(x) \;=\; \sum_{\ell \in B} T\bigl(|F_S(\ell)|\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Partition the sum over keys along the fibres of $b_S$; the inner sum over $F_S(\ell)$
is $T(|L_S(\ell)|) = T(|F_S(\ell)|)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:listcost}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Load conservation]\label{cor:load}
$\sum_{\ell \in B} |F_S(\ell)| = N$.
\end{corollary}

Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting} is the decisive structural fact: the total cost depends on
$S$ only through the multiset of bucket sizes, the \emph{size profile}. Optimising over
schemes is optimising over compositions of $N$ into $m$ non-negative parts.

\section{The arithmetic core: an integral tangent line}

\begin{lemma}[Integral tangent-line inequality]\label{lem:tangent}
For all $k,q \in \mathbb{N}$, computed over $\mathbb{Z}$,
\[
T(q) + (q+1)(k-q) \;\le\; T(k), \qquad
T(k) - \bigl[T(q)+(q+1)(k-q)\bigr] = \frac{(k-q)(k-q-1)}{2}\;\ge\;0 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Multiply by $2$ and use $2T(n)=n(n+1)$: the difference becomes
$k(k+1)-q(q+1)-2(q+1)(k-q) = (k-q)(k-q-1)$, a product of two consecutive integers,
hence non-negative for every integer $k-q$.
\end{proof}

Two features distinguish this from the real tangent at $t=q$ to $t(t+1)/2$, whose slope
is $q+\tfrac12$. First, the slope $q+1$ is an integer, keeping the summed bound in
$\mathbb{Z}$. Second, the slack is $\binom{d}{2}$ with $d=k-q$, and:

\begin{lemma}[Zero locus of the slack]\label{lem:zeros}
For $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, $d(d-1)=0$ if and only if $d \in \{0,1\}$.
\end{lemma}

This double zero is the source of rigidity: a bucket incurs no slack precisely when its
size is $q$ or $q+1$.

\begin{definition}[Optimum function]
For $m \ge 1$ set
$\Opt(N,m) = r\,T(q+1) + (m-r)\,T(q)$, equivalently $\Opt(N,m) = m\,T(q) + r(q+1)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact pigeonhole lower bound]\label{thm:lower}
Let $m \ge 1$ and $f:\{1,\dots,m\}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_i f(i) = N$. Then
$\Opt(N,m) \le \sum_{i=1}^m T(f(i))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent} to each $f(i)$ at the fixed tangent point $q$ and sum:
\[
\sum_i T(f(i)) \ge m\,T(q) + (q+1)\Bigl(\sum_i f(i) - mq\Bigr) = m\,T(q) + (q+1)r
= \Opt(N,m),
\]
using $N - mq = r$. The sum of the tangent lower bounds is independent of $f$, which is
what makes the bound sharp.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Balanced profile]
$f^{\mathrm{bal}}(i) = q + [\,i \le r\,]$ for $1 \le i \le m$: $r$ buckets of size $q+1$
and $m-r$ of size $q$, with $\sum_i f^{\mathrm{bal}}(i) = N$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Attainment]\label{thm:attain}
$\sum_{i=1}^m T\bigl(f^{\mathrm{bal}}(i)\bigr) = \Opt(N,m)$.
\end{theorem}

\section{The exact optimum for scan schemes}

\begin{theorem}[Universal lower bound]\label{thm:univlower}
Every scan scheme $S$ on $N$ keys with $m \ge 1$ bucket labels satisfies
$C(S) \ge \Opt(N,m)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting}, $C(S) = \sum_\ell T(|F_S(\ell)|)$; the sizes sum to $N$
by Corollary~\ref{cor:load}; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:lower} after transporting $B$ to
$\{1,\dots,m\}$ along a bijection.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Residue scheme]
For key set $\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ and $m \ge 1$, the \emph{residue scheme} $R_{N,m}$ has
bucket map $x \mapsto x \bmod m$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Residue counts]\label{lem:residue}
For $0 \le j < m$, the number of $x \in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ with $x \equiv j \pmod m$
equals $q + [\,j < r\,]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $N$: adding the key $N$ increments exactly the class $j = N \bmod m$, and the
update matches the change in $q + [\,j<r\,]$ in both cases (whether or not $N+1$ is a
multiple of $m$).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Residue scheme attains the optimum]\label{thm:residue}
$C(R_{N,m}) = \Opt(N,m)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact optimum]\label{thm:optimum}
For $m \ge 1$, $\Opt(N,m)$ is the least element of
$\{\,C(S) : S \text{ a scan scheme on } N \text{ keys with } m \text{ buckets}\,\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Membership is Theorem~\ref{thm:residue}; minimality is Theorem~\ref{thm:univlower}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
$N=5$, $m=3$: $q=1$, $r=2$, so $\Opt = 2T(2)+T(1) = 7$. Exhaustive enumeration of all
$3^5=243$ schemes returns minimum $7$ and maximum $T(5)=15$.
\end{example}

\section{Rigidity, perfect hashing, and symmetry}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the optimum]\label{thm:rigidity}
Let $m \ge 1$ and $\sum_i f(i)=N$. Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m T(f(i)) = \Opt(N,m) \iff \forall i,\ q \le f(i) \le q+1 .
\]
Consequently a scan scheme $S$ satisfies $C(S) = \Opt(N,m)$ if and only if every bucket
has size $\lfloor N/m\rfloor$ or $\lceil N/m\rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) The difference between the two sides of Theorem~\ref{thm:lower} is
$\sum_i \tfrac12 (f(i)-q)(f(i)-q-1)$, a sum of non-negative integers; if it vanishes,
each term does, and Lemma~\ref{lem:zeros} gives $f(i)-q \in \{0,1\}$.
($\Leftarrow$) If every $f(i) \in \{q,q+1\}$ then $T(f(i)) = T(q) + (f(i)-q)(q+1)$
exactly, and $\sum_i (f(i)-q) = r$, so the sum telescopes to $mT(q)+r(q+1)$. The scheme
statement follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting}.
\end{proof}

Rigidity upgrades optimisation to classification: the optimal locus \emph{consists of}
the balanced schemes, no more and no less.

\begin{theorem}[Perfect hashing]\label{thm:perfect}
For a scan scheme $S$, the following are equivalent: (i) $\cost_S(x)=1$ for every key
$x$; (ii) the bucket map $b_S$ is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii): all indices vanish, so $\enc_S(x) = (b_S(x),0)$, and injectivity
of $\enc_S$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:unique}) forces injectivity of $b_S$.
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i): every fibre containing $x$ is $\{x\}$, so
Corollary~\ref{cor:range} gives $\cost_S(x)=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No collision-free compression]
If $m < N$ then some key has $\cost_S(x) \ge 2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Pigeonhole failure analysis]\label{thm:failure}
If $N \ge 1$ and $B \neq \emptyset$, then some key $x$ satisfies
$N \le m \cdot \cost_S(x)$: some key costs at least the average bucket load.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Some bucket $\ell$ satisfies $N \le m\,|F_S(\ell)|$, for otherwise summing
$m|F_S(\ell)| \le N-1$ over the $m$ buckets contradicts Corollary~\ref{cor:load}. That
bucket is nonempty and its last-scanned key has cost exactly $|F_S(\ell)|$, its index
being $|F_S(\ell)|-1$ by duplicate-freeness of the scan list.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry invariance]\label{thm:symmetry}
For any permutation $\sigma$ of the keys, the scheme with bucket map $b_S \circ \sigma$
has the same total cost as $S$; and for any bijection $e$ of bucket labels, the scheme
with bucket map $e \circ b_S$ has the same total cost as $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting} the cost is a function of the size profile alone.
Pre-composition with $\sigma$ replaces each fibre by an equinumerous preimage;
post-composition with $e$ permutes the fibres.
\end{proof}

Thus $C$ is a class function for the natural $\Sym(A)\times\Sym(B)$ action, and the
optimal locus of Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity} is a single orbit: any two balanced profiles
differ by a permutation of buckets, and any two schemes with the same profile differ by
a permutation of keys.

\begin{remark}[Counting the optimal locus]\label{rem:count}
Orbit--stabiliser then predicts the number of cost-optimal maps
$\{1,\dots,N\}\to\{1,\dots,m\}$ to be
\[
\binom{m}{r}\cdot\frac{N!}{\bigl((q+1)!\bigr)^{r}(q!)^{m-r}} .
\]
For $(N,m)=(5,3)$ this gives $3\cdot 30 = 90$, matching exhaustive enumeration; for
$(7,4)$ it gives $2520$, again matching. See Conjecture~\ref{conj:count}.
\end{remark}

\section{The ceiling and the achievable set}

\begin{lemma}[Superadditivity]\label{lem:super}
For all $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$, $T(a)+T(b) \le T(a+b)$, with difference $ab$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$2T(a+b)-2T(a)-2T(b) = (a+b)(a+b+1)-a(a+1)-b(b+1) = 2ab \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

By induction $\sum_i T(f(i)) \le T\bigl(\sum_i f(i)\bigr)$: merging buckets never
decreases cost.

\begin{theorem}[Universal upper bound and exact maximum]\label{thm:max}
Every scan scheme on $N$ keys satisfies $C(S) \le T(N)$, and the degenerate scheme
placing every key in a single bucket achieves $C = T(N)$. Hence $T(N)$ is the greatest
achievable total cost.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cost window]\label{thm:window}
For $m \ge 1$, every scan scheme on $N$ keys with $m$ buckets satisfies
$\Opt(N,m) \le C(S) \le T(N)$, and both endpoints are attained---by the residue scheme
and by the one-bucket scheme respectively.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[Exact achievable set]\label{prop:achievable}
The set of achievable total costs of scan schemes on $N$ keys with $m$ buckets is
exactly
\[
\Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_i T(k_i) \;:\; (k_i) \text{ a partition of } N \text{ into at most } m \text{ parts}\Bigr\}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting} the cost depends only on the size profile, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetry} the profile may be taken up to reordering, i.e.\ as a
partition of $N$ into at most $m$ parts. Conversely every such partition is realised by
some bucket map.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[The window is porous]\label{ex:porous}
For $(N,m)=(5,3)$ the partitions of $5$ into at most $3$ parts are $2{+}2{+}1$,
$3{+}1{+}1$, $3{+}2$, $4{+}1$, $5$, with costs $7,8,9,11,15$. Exhaustive enumeration
over all $243$ schemes returns exactly $\{7,8,9,11,15\}$: the values $10,12,13,14$
inside the window $[7,15]$ are \emph{not} achievable. For $(6,3)$ the achievable set is
$\{9,10,12,13,16,21\}$ and for $(7,3)$ it is $\{12,13,14,16,17,18,22,28\}$. Hence the
cost spectrum is not a gapless integer interval; the correct statement is
Proposition~\ref{prop:achievable}.
\end{example}

\section{The mean cost and the $\varepsilon$-compression barrier}

\begin{theorem}[Division-free averaged optimum]\label{thm:divfree}
For $m \ge 1$ and $N \ge 0$, $\;N(N+m) \le 2m\,\Opt(N,m)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $N = mq+r$, $0 \le r < m$, and $\Opt(N,m) = mT(q)+r(q+1)$, $2T(q)=q(q+1)$:
\[
2m\,\Opt(N,m) = m^2q(q+1) + 2mr(q+1) = m(q+1)(mq+2r),
\]
while $N(N+m) = (mq+r)(mq+r+m)$. Expanding and subtracting, all quadratic terms in $q$
cancel and one is left with $2m\,\Opt(N,m) - N(N+m) = 2mr - r^2 - mr = r(m-r) \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

The defect $r(m-r)$ vanishes precisely when $r=0$, i.e.\ when $m \mid N$.

\begin{theorem}[Mean-cost lower bound]\label{thm:mean}
For $N \ge 1$, $m \ge 1$ and any scan scheme $S$,
\[
\frac{C(S)}{N} \;\ge\; \frac12\left(\frac{N}{m}+1\right),
\]
with real division.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:univlower} gives $C(S) \ge \Opt(N,m)$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:divfree}
gives $2m\Opt(N,m) \ge N(N+m)$; hence $2m\,C(S) \ge N(N+m)$, i.e.\
$C(S)/N \ge (N+m)/(2m)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\varepsilon$-compression barrier]\label{thm:barrier}
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and suppose $m \le \varepsilon N$. Then
$\dfrac{C(S)}{N} \ge \dfrac{1}{2\varepsilon}$ for every scan scheme $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$m \le \varepsilon N$ gives $N/m \ge 1/\varepsilon$; substitute in
Theorem~\ref{thm:mean} and discard the additive $\tfrac12$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sharp}
If $m \mid N$ and $m \ge 1$, then $2m\,C(R_{N,m}) = N(N+m)$: the residue scheme meets
Theorem~\ref{thm:mean} with equality, so the constant $1/2$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:barrier} cannot be improved.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $N = mq$ then $r=0$ and $\Opt(N,m) = mT(q)$, so
$2m\,C(R_{N,m}) = 2m^2T(q) = m^2q(q+1) = (mq)(mq+m) = N(N+m)$.
\end{proof}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Interpretation.} Space and time multiply. Using an $\varepsilon$ fraction as
many buckets as keys forces an average of at least $1/(2\varepsilon)$ comparisons per
lookup; the product (space fraction) $\times$ (mean lookup cost) is at least $1/2$,
uniformly over all schemes, key sets and orderings. With $N=4096$ and $m=256$
($\varepsilon = 1/16$) the barrier gives $8$, the exact bound gives $8.5$, and the
residue scheme achieves exactly $8.5$.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Exact optimum]
Given $N$, $m \ge 1$, compute $q = \lfloor N/m\rfloor$, $r = N \bmod m$ and return
$r\,T(q+1)+(m-r)\,T(q)$. Cost $O(1)$; correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:optimum}.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Optimality test by rigidity]
Given a bucket map on $N$ keys with $m$ buckets, compute the size profile in $O(N+m)$
time and accept iff every size lies in $\{\lfloor N/m\rfloor,\lceil N/m\rceil\}$.
Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity}. Unlike computing the cost and comparing, the
test names an offending bucket when it rejects.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Achievable-cost enumeration]
Enumerate the partitions of $N$ into at most $m$ parts and record $\sum_i T(k_i)$ for
each. By Proposition~\ref{prop:achievable} this yields the exact achievable cost set, at
a cost proportional to the number of such partitions---vastly cheaper than the $m^N$
brute-force enumeration over schemes.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Discussion and future work}

\subsection{What is gained by exactness}
The classical treatment replaces the bucket map by a random function and reports
expectations. That predicts the behaviour of a typical hash function but cannot answer
design questions: what is the best a scheme could do, which schemes achieve it, how many
are there, and what does compression cost in the worst case? Every result above is
deterministic and exact. In particular the compression barrier is not an average-case
heuristic: it holds for every scheme, every key set and every scan order.

\subsection{Applications}
\emph{Index sizing.} Theorem~\ref{thm:barrier} gives a design rule: a budget of $c$
comparisons on average requires at least $N/(2c)$ buckets, however clever the
assignment; and by Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} the naive residue assignment already meets
that budget when it divides evenly.
\emph{Load-balancing certificates.} The rigidity test turns ``is my table optimally
balanced?'' into an $O(N+m)$ certificate check with a precise failure witness rather
than a statistical goodness-of-fit test.
\emph{Code design.} Theorem~\ref{thm:unique} identifies (bucket, index) as a uniquely
decodable code, and the cost model counts exactly the work of the induced sequential
decoder---a deterministic analogue of the coding-theoretic trade-off between codeword
length and decoding effort.

\subsection{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Enumerative rigidity]\label{conj:count}
The number of cost-optimal bucket maps $\{1,\dots,N\}\to\{1,\dots,m\}$ is exactly
$\binom{m}{r}\,N!\,/\,\bigl((q+1)!\bigr)^{r}(q!)^{m-r}$ with $q=\lfloor N/m\rfloor$,
$r = N \bmod m$. Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity} identifies the optimal locus with the
balanced profiles and Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetry} shows the symmetry group acts, so the
count should follow from orbit--stabiliser. Confirmed by exhaustive enumeration for
$(N,m) = (5,3)$, $(6,3)$ and $(7,4)$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{problem}[Structure of the achievable set]
Proposition~\ref{prop:achievable} identifies the achievable costs with sums of
triangular numbers over partitions of $N$ into at most $m$ parts, and
Example~\ref{ex:porous} shows this set has gaps. Determine the gap structure exactly.
Transferring one key from a bucket of size $a$ to one of size $b$ changes the cost by
exactly $b+1-a$, so the achievable set is the orbit of the balanced profile under unit
moves; a plausible precise statement is that it is gapless on an initial segment
$[\Opt(N,m), B(N,m)]$ for an explicit threshold $B(N,m)$, and sparse above it.
\end{problem}

\begin{conjecture}[Two-level schemes and the barrier]
Iterating the construction---a bucket map into $m_1$ buckets followed by a second bucket
map into $m_2$ sub-buckets inside each---cannot beat the one-level barrier at equal
total space: for every two-level scheme with $m_1m_2 \le \varepsilon N$ sub-buckets, the
mean decoding cost is at least $1/(2\varepsilon)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:accounting} applies
verbatim at each level, the cost of the refined structure again being a sum of
triangular numbers over the finest fibres.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{problem}[Weighted keys]
Replace the uniform access distribution by weights $w(x)\ge 0$ and minimise
$\sum_x w(x)\cost_S(x)$. Within a bucket the optimal scan order is by decreasing weight,
so the problem becomes a weighted partition problem; the convexity mechanism should be
replaced by a majorisation argument, and it is unclear whether an exact closed form
survives.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Beyond linear scan]
Replace the intra-bucket linear scan by binary search, so that a bucket of size $k$ costs
$\sum_{j<k}\bigl(1+\lfloor \log_2 j\rfloor\bigr)$. This is still convex but no longer
polynomial; the tangent-line method should still yield an exact optimum with a modified
balanced profile, and the corresponding barrier would degrade from $1/(2\varepsilon)$ to
$\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
\end{problem}

\section{Conclusion}

Bucketed lookup, analysed exactly rather than asymptotically, is a small and complete
theory. An honest cost model---one in which the pair (bucket label, intra-bucket index)
is proved to be a uniquely decodable address---reduces, by an exact accounting identity,
to the minimisation of $\sum_i T(k_i)$ over compositions of $N$ into $m$ parts. A single
integral tangent line with slope $\lfloor N/m\rfloor+1$ delivers the exact optimum
$r\,T(q+1)+(m-r)\,T(q)$; the double zero of its slack delivers rigidity; the resulting
symmetry orbit delivers a counting formula; superadditivity delivers the ceiling $T(N)$;
and averaging delivers the space--time barrier $1/(2\varepsilon)$ with the sharp
constant $1/2$. The remaining open questions---counting the optimal locus, describing
the gaps in the achievable set, and extending the barrier to hierarchical schemes---are
all reachable from the same two facts: costs are triangular, and triangles are convex.

Scan schemes: honest uniqueness decoding, exact cost accounting,
the pigeonhole optimum, rigidity, and the 1/(2*eps) compression barrier.

Everything in this file is self-contained (standard library only) and mirrors,
numerically, the theorems of the accompanying paper:

  * triangle(k) = k(k+1)/2 is the cost of scanning every key of a bucket of size k;
  * total cost of a scheme = sum over buckets of triangle(bucket size)  (exact);
  * min over all schemes = triangleOpt(N, m)
        = r * triangle(q+1) + (m-r) * triangle(q),   q = N // m, r = N % m;
  * the residue scheme x |-> x mod m attains it;
  * a scheme is optimal iff every bucket has size q or q+1 (rigidity);
  * max over all schemes = triangle(N), attained by the one-bucket scheme;
  * mean cost >= (N/m + 1)/2, hence >= 1/(2*eps) whenever m <= eps*N.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Dict, Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Triangular cost and the exact optimum
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def triangle(k: int) -> int:
    """triangle(k) = 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2, the cost of scanning a bucket of size k."""
    return k * (k + 1) // 2


def triangle_opt(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """The exact minimal total decoding cost of n keys in m buckets."""
    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("m must be positive")
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return r * triangle(q + 1) + (m - r) * triangle(q)


def balanced_profile(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The balanced bucket-size profile: r buckets of size q+1, m-r of size q."""
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return [q + 1 if i < r else q for i in range(m)]


def tangent_slack(k: int, q: int) -> int:
    """triangle(k) - [triangle(q) + (q+1)(k-q)] = (k-q)(k-q-1)/2 >= 0."""
    d = k - q
    return d * (d - 1) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Scan schemes: encoding, decoding, exact cost
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class ScanScheme:
    """A scan scheme on keys 0..n-1 with m buckets, given by a bucket map."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, m: int, bucket_map: Sequence[int]) -> None:
        if len(bucket_map) != n:
            raise ValueError("bucket_map must have one entry per key")
        if any(not (0 <= b < m) for b in bucket_map):
            raise ValueError("bucket labels out of range")
        self.n: int = n
        self.m: int = m
        self.bucket: List[int] = list(bucket_map)

    def fiber(self, b: int) -> List[int]:
        """The keys stored in bucket b, in the order in which a scan visits them."""
        return [x for x in range(self.n) if self.bucket[x] == b]

    def scan_list(self, b: int) -> List[int]:
        """Alias for the fiber, emphasising that it is an ordered scan sequence."""
        return self.fiber(b)

    def idx(self, x: int) -> int:
        """The intra-bucket index of key x: its 0-based position in its own bucket."""
        return self.scan_list(self.bucket[x]).index(x)

    def decode_cost(self, x: int) -> int:
        """1-based number of comparisons a scan performs to find x."""
        return self.idx(x) + 1

    def encode(self, x: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
        """The scan code of x: (bucket label, intra-bucket index)."""
        return (self.bucket[x], self.idx(x))

    def decode(self, code: Tuple[int, int]) -> int | None:
        """Read off the entry at the given index of the given bucket, if any."""
        b, i = code
        lst = self.scan_list(b)
        return lst[i] if 0 <= i < len(lst) else None

    def profile(self) -> List[int]:
        """The bucket-size profile of the scheme."""
        return [len(self.fiber(b)) for b in range(self.m)]

    def total_cost(self) -> int:
        """Total decoding cost, summed over all keys."""
        return sum(self.decode_cost(x) for x in range(self.n))

    def mean_cost(self) -> float:
        return self.total_cost() / self.n if self.n else 0.0


def mod_scheme(n: int, m: int) -> ScanScheme:
    """The residue scheme: key x is stored in bucket x mod m."""
    return ScanScheme(n, m, [x % m for x in range(n)])


def const_scheme(n: int, m: int) -> ScanScheme:
    """The degenerate scheme: every key in bucket 0."""
    return ScanScheme(n, m, [0] * n)


def all_schemes(n: int, m: int) -> Iterator[ScanScheme]:
    """Enumerate all m^n scan schemes (only for tiny n, m)."""
    for bm in product(range(m), repeat=n):
        yield ScanScheme(n, m, bm)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Checks corresponding to the theorems
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_honest_decoding(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    """decode(encode(x)) = x, and (b,i) decodes to x iff (b,i) = encode(x)."""
    for x in range(scheme.n):
        if scheme.decode(scheme.encode(x)) != x:
            return False
    for b in range(scheme.m):
        for i in range(scheme.n + 1):
            y = scheme.decode((b, i))
            if y is not None and (b, i) != scheme.encode(y):
                return False
    return True


def check_cost_accounting(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    """Total cost equals the sum of triangular numbers of the bucket sizes."""
    return scheme.total_cost() == sum(triangle(k) for k in scheme.profile())


def is_balanced(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    q = scheme.n // scheme.m
    return all(q <= k <= q + 1 for k in scheme.profile())


def brute_force_extremes(n: int, m: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    costs = [s.total_cost() for s in all_schemes(n, m)]
    return min(costs), max(costs)


def achievable_costs(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    return sorted({s.total_cost() for s in all_schemes(n, m)})


def partitions_into_at_most(n: int, m: int, cap: int | None = None) -> Iterator[List[int]]:
    """All multisets of at most m positive parts summing to n, in weakly decreasing order."""
    if cap is None:
        cap = n
    if n == 0:
        yield []
        return
    if m == 0:
        return
    for part in range(min(n, cap), 0, -1):
        for rest in partitions_into_at_most(n - part, m - 1, part):
            yield [part] + rest


def partition_costs(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The predicted achievable cost set: sums of triangular numbers over size profiles."""
    return sorted({sum(triangle(k) for k in p) for p in partitions_into_at_most(n, m)})


def count_optimal_schemes(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    opt = triangle_opt(n, m)
    return sum(1 for s in all_schemes(n, m) if s.total_cost() == opt)


def predicted_optimal_count(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """C(m, r) * multinomial(n; q+1 repeated r times, q repeated m-r times)."""
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    multinomial = factorial(n) // (factorial(q + 1) ** r * factorial(q) ** (m - r))
    return comb(m, r) * multinomial

# 4. Reporting

    n, m = 12, 5

    print("bucket profile:", s.profile())

    print(" key | bucket | index | code    | decode(code) | cost")
    print("-----+--------+-------+---------+--------------+-----")

    print("total cost              :", s.total_cost())
    print("sum of triangle(sizes)  :", sum(triangle(k) for k in s.profile()))
    print("exact accounting holds  :", check_cost_accounting(s))


def demo_optimum() -> None:
    section("2. The exact pigeonhole optimum, verified by brute force")
    print(" N   m | triangleOpt | brute-force min | triangle(N) | brute-force max")

from itertools import product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Dict, Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Triangular cost and the exact optimum
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def triangle(k: int) -> int:
    """triangle(k) = 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2, the cost of scanning a bucket of size k."""
    return k * (k + 1) // 2


def triangle_opt(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """The exact minimal total decoding cost of n keys in m buckets."""
    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("m must be positive")
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return r * triangle(q + 1) + (m - r) * triangle(q)


def balanced_profile(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The balanced bucket-size profile: r buckets of size q+1, m-r of size q."""
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return [q + 1 if i < r else q for i in range(m)]


def tangent_slack(k: int, q: int) -> int:
    """triangle(k) - [triangle(q) + (q+1)(k-q)] = (k-q)(k-q-1)/2 >= 0."""
    d = k - q
    return d * (d - 1) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Scan schemes: encoding, decoding, exact cost
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class ScanScheme:
    """A scan scheme on keys 0..n-1 with m buckets, given by a bucket map."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, m: int, bucket_map: Sequence[int]) -> None:
        if len(bucket_map) != n:
            raise ValueError("bucket_map must have one entry per key")
        if any(not (0 <= b < m) for b in bucket_map):
            raise ValueError("bucket labels out of range")
        self.n: int = n
        self.m: int = m
        self.bucket: List[int] = list(bucket_map)

    def fiber(self, b: int) -> List[int]:
        """The keys stored in bucket b, in the order in which a scan visits them."""
        return [x for x in range(self.n) if self.bucket[x] == b]

    def scan_list(self, b: int) -> List[int]:
        """Alias for the fiber, emphasising that it is an ordered scan sequence."""
        return self.fiber(b)

    def idx(self, x: int) -> int:
        """The intra-bucket index of key x: its 0-based position in its own bucket."""
        return self.scan_list(self.bucket[x]).index(x)

    def decode_cost(self, x: int) -> int:
        """1-based number of comparisons a scan performs to find x."""
        return self.idx(x) + 1

    def encode(self, x: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
        """The scan code of x: (bucket label, intra-bucket index)."""
        return (self.bucket[x], self.idx(x))

    def decode(self, code: Tuple[int, int]) -> int | None:
        """Read off the entry at the given index of the given bucket, if any."""
        b, i = code
        lst = self.scan_list(b)
        return lst[i] if 0 <= i < len(lst) else None

    def profile(self) -> List[int]:
        """The bucket-size profile of the scheme."""
        return [len(self.fiber(b)) for b in range(self.m)]

    def total_cost(self) -> int:
        """Total decoding cost, summed over all keys."""
        return sum(self.decode_cost(x) for x in range(self.n))

    def mean_cost(self) -> float:
        return self.total_cost() / self.n if self.n else 0.0


def mod_scheme(n: int, m: int) -> ScanScheme:
    """The residue scheme: key x is stored in bucket x mod m."""
    return ScanScheme(n, m, [x % m for x in range(n)])


def const_scheme(n: int, m: int) -> ScanScheme:
    """The degenerate scheme: every key in bucket 0."""
    return ScanScheme(n, m, [0] * n)


def all_schemes(n: int, m: int) -> Iterator[ScanScheme]:
    """Enumerate all m^n scan schemes (only for tiny n, m)."""
    for bm in product(range(m), repeat=n):
        yield ScanScheme(n, m, bm)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Checks corresponding to the theorems
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_honest_decoding(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    """decode(encode(x)) = x, and (b,i) decodes to x iff (b,i) = encode(x)."""
    for x in range(scheme.n):
        if scheme.decode(scheme.encode(x)) != x:
            return False
    for b in range(scheme.m):
        for i in range(scheme.n + 1):
            y = scheme.decode((b, i))
            if y is not None and (b, i) != scheme.encode(y):
                return False
    return True


def check_cost_accounting(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    """Total cost equals the sum of triangular numbers of the bucket sizes."""
    return scheme.total_cost() == sum(triangle(k) for k in scheme.profile())


def is_balanced(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    q = scheme.n // scheme.m
    return all(q <= k <= q + 1 for k in scheme.profile())


def brute_force_extremes(n: int, m: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    costs = [s.total_cost() for s in all_schemes(n, m)]
    return min(costs), max(costs)


def achievable_costs(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    return sorted({s.total_cost() for s in all_schemes(n, m)})


def partitions_into_at_most(n: int, m: int, cap: int | None = None) -> Iterator[List[int]]:
    """All multisets of at most m positive parts summing to n, in weakly decreasing order."""
    if cap is None:
        cap = n
    if n == 0:
        yield []
        return
    if m == 0:
        return
    for part in range(min(n, cap), 0, -1):
        for rest in partitions_into_at_most(n - part, m - 1, part):
            yield [part] + rest


def partition_costs(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The predicted achievable cost set: sums of triangular numbers over size profiles."""
    return sorted({sum(triangle(k) for k in p) for p in partitions_into_at_most(n, m)})


def count_optimal_schemes(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    opt = triangle_opt(n, m)
    return sum(1 for s in all_schemes(n, m) if s.total_cost() == opt)


def predicted_optimal_count(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """C(m, r) * multinomial(n; q+1 repeated r times, q repeated m-r times)."""
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    multinomial = factorial(n) // (factorial(q + 1) ** r * factorial(q) ** (m - r))
    return comb(m, r) * multinomial

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations, product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def triangle(k: int) -> int:
    return k * (k + 1) // 2


def exact_optimum(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return r * triangle(q + 1) + (m - r) * triangle(q)


def profile(bucket_map: Tuple[int, ...], m: int) -> List[int]:
    sizes = [0] * m
    for b in bucket_map:
        sizes[b] += 1
    return sizes


def cost(bucket_map: Tuple[int, ...], m: int) -> int:
    return sum(triangle(k) for k in profile(bucket_map, m))


def is_balanced(bucket_map: Tuple[int, ...], m: int) -> bool:
    q = len(bucket_map) // m
    return all(q <= k <= q + 1 for k in profile(bucket_map, m))


def orbit_count(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    multinomial = factorial(n) // (factorial(q + 1) ** r * factorial(q) ** (m - r))
    return comb(m, r) * multinomial

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def triangle(k: int) -> int:
    return k * (k + 1) // 2


def triangle_opt(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return r * triangle(q + 1) + (m - r) * triangle(q)


def partitions(n: int, parts: int, cap: int) -> Iterator[List[int]]:
    if n == 0:
        yield []
        return
    if parts == 0:

    for p in range(min(n, cap), 0, -1):

    return sorted({sum(triangle(k) for k in p) for p in partitions(n, m, n)})

    ax.margins(x=0.18)

    fig.savefig("scan_scheme_spectrum.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote scan_scheme_spectrum.png")

  "interactive_layout": "# Scan Schemes: the exact price of looking things up

Somewhere in the machine you are reading this on, a piece of software is looking something
up: which glyph belongs to a character code, where a database row lives, whether an
identifier has been declared. Almost all of them use the same ancient trick — throw the keys
into a modest number of labelled boxes, and when you need a key, open its box and look
through it.

This page is a guided tour of what that trick costs, **exactly**. Not asymptotically, not up
to a constant: exactly, with the optimum identified, the optimal schemes classified, and the
space–time trade-off pinned to the constant $1/2$.

---

## 1. The model in one paragraph

Fix $N$ keys, totally ordered, and $m$ bucket labels. A **scan scheme** is just a map
$\beta$ from keys to bucket labels — no randomness, no assumptions about the keys. To find a
key you scan its bucket in order and compare until you hit it, so the **decoding cost** of a
key is its (1-based) position inside its own bucket. The object of study is the **total
decoding cost** $C = \sum_x \mathrm{cost}(x)$: the price of retrieving every key once, or
equivalently $N$ times the average lookup cost.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the ordering inside a bucket does not matter</b> (click to expand)</summary>

A scan of a bucket holding $k$ keys retrieves those $k$ keys at costs $1, 2, \dots, k$ — in
some order, but always exactly those costs. So re-ordering a bucket permutes which key pays
what, and leaves the total unchanged. That is why the theory only ever sees the *sizes* of
the buckets, never their contents. Every statement below is a consequence of that single
observation, made precise.
</details>

---

## 2. Play first: the Bucket Laboratory

Before any theorem, get your hands dirty. Slide $N$ and $m$, move keys between buckets, and
watch the total cost respond. Try to beat the "Balance" button — you cannot, and the widget
tells you exactly how much each off-balance bucket is costing you.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Two things to notice while you play:

1. The cost only ever depends on **how many** keys are in each bucket, never on which ones.
2. The minimum is hit precisely when every bucket holds $\lfloor N/m \rfloor$ or
   $\lceil N/m \rceil$ keys. Any other arrangement is strictly worse.

Both observations are theorems. Let us see why.

---

## 3. Is the cost model honest?

A lower bound is only as good as the guarantee that the thing being counted is real. Here the
thing we must not fudge is that a scan really *identifies* a key. Define the **scan code** of
a key $x$ to be the pair
$$\mathrm{enc}(x) = \bigl(\beta(x),\, i(x)\bigr),$$
where $i(x)$ is the **intra-bucket index**: the position of $x$ inside the ordered list of
its own bucket. Decoding a pair $(b,i)$ means: go to bucket $b$, return its $i$-th entry if
there is one.

> **Honest Uniqueness Decoding.** For every key $x$, the code $\mathrm{enc}(x)$ decodes to
> $x$; and for every pair $(b,i)$ and key $x$, the pair $(b,i)$ decodes to $x$ **if and only
> if** $(b,i) = \mathrm{enc}(x)$. In particular the encoding is injective.

Probe it yourself — pick any address and see what comes out, including addresses that are out
of range:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>The proof, in three lines</b></summary>

A bucket's contents form a duplicate-free list. In such a list the position of an element
determines the element (read the entry), and the element determines the position (there is
only one occurrence). So encoding and decoding are mutually inverse where both are defined,
and out-of-range indices decode to nothing at all rather than to a wrong key. Injectivity is
immediate: apply the decoder to an equality of codes.
</details>

The same widget also demonstrates the second pillar, which the panel at the bottom checks
live:

> **Exact Cost Accounting.** $\displaystyle \sum_x \mathrm{cost}(x) = \sum_b T\bigl(|\beta^{-1}(b)|\bigr)$,
> where $T(k) = k(k+1)/2 = 1 + 2 + \cdots + k$.

This identity is the hinge of the whole subject: it converts a question about comparisons and
orderings into a question about a *list of bucket sizes*.

---

## 4. One tangent line does all the work

We now have to minimise $T(k_1) + \cdots + T(k_m)$ subject to $k_1 + \cdots + k_m = N$. The
tool is a discrete convexity statement with an integer twist.

> **Integral Tangent-Line Inequality.** For all integers $k, q \ge 0$,
> $$T(q) + (q+1)(k-q) \le T(k), \qquad \text{with slack } \frac{(k-q)(k-q-1)}{2}.$$

The slope $q+1$ is an *integer*, unlike the real tangent slope $q + \tfrac12$, and the slack
is a product of two consecutive integers — so it is never negative, and it is zero exactly
twice: at $k = q$ and at $k = q + 1$.

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>How this yields the exact optimum</b></summary>

Sum the inequality over all $m$ buckets with the tangent point $q = \lfloor N/m \rfloor$. The
linear terms collapse, because $\sum_i k_i = N$ regardless of the scheme, so the sum of the
tangent values is a constant:
$$\sum_i T(k_i) \;\ge\; m\,T(q) + (q+1)\bigl(N - mq\bigr) \;=\; m\,T(q) + r(q+1),
\qquad r = N \bmod m.$$
That constant is $\mathrm{Opt}(N,m) = r\,T(q+1) + (m-r)\,T(q)$. And it is *attained*: the
residue scheme $x \mapsto x \bmod m$ has exactly $r$ buckets of size $q+1$ and $m-r$ of size
$q$. So the bound is not a bound at all — it is the optimum.
</details>

> **The Exact Optimum.** The least total decoding cost of $N$ keys in $m$ buckets is
> $$\mathrm{Opt}(N,m) = r\,T(q+1) + (m-r)\,T(q), \qquad q = \lfloor N/m\rfloor,\ r = N\bmod m,$$
> attained by the residue scheme $x \mapsto x \bmod m$.

And constructing an optimal scheme, with its uniquely decodable index, takes linear time:

---

## 5. Rigidity: from optimisation to classification

Because the total slack is a sum of non-negative terms, the bound is met with equality
exactly when *every* slack vanishes — and we know precisely when a slack vanishes.

> **Rigidity of the Optimum.** A scheme costs exactly $\mathrm{Opt}(N,m)$ if and only if
> every bucket holds $\lfloor N/m\rfloor$ or $\lceil N/m\rceil$ keys.

This is the difference between folklore and theorem: the optimal schemes are not merely
*among* the balanced ones, they *are* the balanced ones. That turns optimality checking into
an $O(N+m)$ certificate that even names the offending bucket when it fails:

{{algorithm:2}}

Two companion facts complete the structural picture.

> **Symmetry Invariance.** Permuting the keys before the bucket map, or relabelling the
> buckets, leaves the total cost unchanged.
>
> **Perfect Hashing.** Every key costs exactly one comparison if and only if the bucket map is
> injective. Hence if there are fewer buckets than keys, some key costs at least two — no
> compressing scheme is collision-free.
>
> **Failure Analysis.** In every scheme some key $x$ satisfies $N \le m \cdot \mathrm{cost}(x)$:
> somebody always pays at least the average load.

<details>
<summary><b>Why symmetry plus rigidity should let us <i>count</i> the optimal schemes</b></summary>

Symmetry says the cost is a class function for the action of
$\mathrm{Sym}(\text{keys}) \times \mathrm{Sym}(\text{buckets})$, and rigidity says the optimal
locus is exactly the balanced profiles. Any two balanced profiles differ by a permutation of
buckets, and any two schemes with the same profile differ by a permutation of keys — so the
optimal locus is a *single orbit*. Orbit–stabiliser then predicts
$$\#\{\text{optimal schemes}\} \;=\; \binom{m}{r}\cdot\frac{N!}{\bigl((q+1)!\bigr)^{r}(q!)^{m-r}}.$$
For $N=5$, $m=3$ that is $3 \cdot 30 = 90$; exhaustive enumeration finds exactly $90$. This is
the natural next theorem, and it exists only because rigidity has an "only if" half.
</details>

Run the exhaustive check yourself — it verifies rigidity, the orbit count and symmetry
invariance simultaneously on every one of the $m^N$ schemes for small instances:

{{demo:1}}

---

## 6. The ceiling, and the surprise inside the window

Convexity gave the floor; **superadditivity** $T(a) + T(b) \le T(a+b)$ gives the ceiling.
Merging buckets never helps, so the worst thing you can do is put everything in one bucket:

> **The Cost Window.** Every scheme on $N$ keys with $m \ge 1$ buckets has total cost in
> $[\mathrm{Opt}(N,m),\ T(N)]$, and both endpoints are realised.

It is tempting to assume everything in between occurs. It does not. Because the cost depends
only on the multiset of bucket sizes, the achievable totals are precisely the sums
$\sum_i T(k_i)$ over partitions of $N$ into at most $m$ parts — a sparse set. Watch the gaps
appear:

{{interactive_demo:2}}

For $N=5$, $m=3$ the achievable totals are $\{7, 8, 9, 11, 15\}$: the window is $[7,15]$, both
ends occur, and $10, 12, 13, 14$ are impossible. Enumerating the spectrum via partitions
instead of via all $m^N$ schemes is an enormous saving:

{{algorithm:3}}

{{visualization:2}}

---

## 7. The punchline: what compression costs

Divide the optimum by $N$ and clear the floor function, and the trade-off appears in the form
an engineer would tape to a wall.

> **Mean-Cost Lower Bound.** Every scheme satisfies
> $\displaystyle \frac{1}{N}\sum_x \mathrm{cost}(x) \ \ge\ \frac{1}{2}\Bigl(\frac{N}{m} + 1\Bigr).$
>
> **The $\varepsilon$-Compression Barrier.** If $m \le \varepsilon N$, then the mean decoding
> cost is at least $\dfrac{1}{2\varepsilon}$.

Space $\varepsilon$, time $1/(2\varepsilon)$: their product never drops below $1/2$. And the
constant is sharp — whenever $m$ divides $N$, the residue scheme meets the mean-cost bound
with equality.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>The two-line derivation</b></summary>

Writing $N = mq + r$, one checks the exact identity
$$2m\,\mathrm{Opt}(N,m) - N(N+m) = r(m-r) \;\ge\; 0,$$
so $2m\,C \ge 2m\,\mathrm{Opt}(N,m) \ge N(N+m)$ for every scheme, i.e.\
$C/N \ge (N+m)/(2m) = \tfrac12(N/m + 1)$. Substituting $N/m \ge 1/\varepsilon$ and discarding
the additive $\tfrac12$ gives the barrier. The defect $r(m-r)$ vanishes exactly when
$m \mid N$ — which is why the residue scheme is then exactly on the floor.
</details>

## 8. Everything at once

The complete numerical companion walks through all eight results in order: honest decoding,
exact accounting, the optimum, the tangent slack, rigidity and the orbit count, the porous
spectrum, perfect hashing, the barrier, and symmetry invariance.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 9. What to take away

Three ideas outlast the arithmetic.

**Honesty in a cost model.** It is easy to prove impressive lower bounds about a model that
cannot be implemented. Insisting up front that the address a scan produces is a genuine,
uniquely decodable code means the bound applies to real lookups.

**Exactness.** Almost everything here is an identity or a sharp inequality with an attainment:
not $O(N^2/m)$ but $r\,T(q+1) + (m-r)\,T(q)$; not "roughly balanced is best" but "balanced,
and nothing else". Exactness is what makes the constant $1/2$ meaningful.

**Rigidity as a gateway.** Once the optimal schemes are *classified*, you can count them, and
you can certify optimality in linear time with a witness.

# The `ε`-compression barrier for scan indices

The exact pigeonhole optimum of `Algebra.ScanSchemeDecoding.Triangle` is stated with the
*floor* `⌊N/m⌋`.  Here we sharpen it to a statement with genuine (real) division, which

namespace ScanSchemeDecoding

open Finset

/-- Exact, division-free form of the averaged optimum. -/
theorem triangleOpt_mul_ge {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) (N : ℕ) :
    N * (N + m) ≤ 2 * m * triangleOpt N m := by
  rw [triangleOpt_eq hm]
  have hN := Nat.div_add_mod N m
  have hr : N % m < m := Nat.mod_lt _ hm
  have h2 := two_mul_triangle (N / m)
  set q := N / m with hqdef
  set r := N % m with hrdef
  set T := triangle q with hTdef
  clear_value T
  clear_value q r
  subst hN
  obtain ⟨s, hs⟩ : ∃ s, m = s + r := ⟨m - r, by omega⟩
  subst hs
  have hexp : 2 * (s + r) * ((s + r) * T + r * (q + 1))
      = (s + r) * ((s + r) * (2 * T)) + 2 * (s + r) * r * (q + 1) := by ring
  rw [hexp, h2]
  nlinarith [Nat.zero_le (r * s), Nat.zero_le q, Nat.zero_le r, Nat.zero_le s]

namespace ScanScheme

variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [LinearOrder α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq β]
variable (S : ScanScheme α β)

/-- Division-free averaged bound for an arbitrary scan scheme. -/
theorem card_mul_ge (hβ : 0 < Fintype.card β) :
    Fintype.card α * (Fintype.card α + Fintype.card β)
      ≤ 2 * Fintype.card β * ∑ x, S.decodeCost x :=
  le_trans (triangleOpt_mul_ge hβ (Fintype.card α))
    (Nat.mul_le_mul_left _ (S.triangleOpt_le_decodeCost hβ))

/-- **Mean-cost lower bound.**  The average number of comparisons per decoded key is at
least `(N/m + 1)/2`, with *exact* real division. -/
theorem mean_decodeCost_ge (hα : 0 < Fintype.card α) (hβ : 0 < Fintype.card β) :

      ≤ (∑ x, S.decodeCost x : ℝ) / (Fintype.card α : ℝ) := by
  have hNpos : (0 : ℝ) < (Fintype.card α : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hα
  have hmpos : (0 : ℝ) < (Fintype.card β : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hβ
  have hkey : (Fintype.card α : ℝ) * ((Fintype.card α : ℝ) + (Fintype.card β : ℝ))

  rw [div_mul_eq_mul_div, div_le_iff₀ hmpos]
  push_cast at hkey ⊢
  nlinarith [hkey, hNpos, hmpos]

# Scan schemes: honest uniqueness decoding and exact cost accounting

A **scan scheme** on a finite key type `α` with bucket labels in `β` is nothing but a
bucket map `bucket : α → β`.  Decoding a key means scanning its bucket, in the
canonical (linear) order, until the key is found.  Two things are then formalised
here, and both are *exact*, not asymptotic:

* **Honest uniqueness decoding** (`ScanScheme.honest_scanCode`,
  `ScanScheme.decode_eq_some_iff`).  The pair `encode x = (bucket x, idx x)`
  — bucket label together with the *intra-bucket index* — decodes back to `x`, and
  it is the **only** pair that does so.  So `encode` is an injection into
  `β × ℕ` whose decoding is unambiguous: no scheme-level ambiguity is hidden in the
  cost model.
* **Exact cost accounting** (`ScanScheme.decodeCost_eq`).  The total decoding cost
  `∑ x, decodeCost x` equals `∑ b, triangle (fiber b).card` *on the nose*.

arithmetic problem solved in `Algebra.ScanSchemeDecoding.Triangle`.

namespace ScanSchemeDecoding

open Finset

/-- A scan scheme: a bucket assignment of keys `α` to bucket labels `β`. -/
structure ScanScheme (α β : Type*) where
  /-- The bucket a key is stored in. -/
  bucket : α → β

variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [LinearOrder α] [DecidableEq β]

namespace ScanScheme

variable (S : ScanScheme α β)

/-- The set of keys stored in bucket `b`. -/
def fiber (b : β) : Finset α := {x | S.bucket x = b}

/-- The keys of bucket `b`, in the order in which a scan visits them. -/
def scanList (b : β) : List α := (S.fiber b).sort (· ≤ ·)

/-- The **intra-bucket index** of a key: its position in the scan of its own bucket. -/
def idx (x : α) : ℕ := (S.scanList (S.bucket x)).idxOf x

/-- Decoding cost: the (1-based) number of comparisons a scan performs to find `x`. -/
def decodeCost (x : α) : ℕ := S.idx x + 1

/-- The scan code of a key: bucket label plus intra-bucket index. -/
def encode (x : α) : β × ℕ := (S.bucket x, S.idx x)

/-- Decoding a scan code: read off the entry at the given index of the given bucket. -/
def decode (p : β × ℕ) : Option α := (S.scanList p.1)[p.2]?

/-!
# The cost spectrum of scan schemes

The exact optimum pins down the *bottom* of the achievable total-cost spectrum.  Here we
pin down the *top*: the triangular number `triangle N` of the whole key set, attained by
the degenerate one-bucket scheme.  The mechanism is the exact opposite of convexity used
for the optimum, namely superadditivity `triangle a + triangle b ≤ triangle (a + b)`.

## Main results

* `ScanSchemeDecoding.triangle_add_le` — superadditivity of the triangular cost.
* `ScanSchemeDecoding.sum_triangle_le` — a scan scheme never costs more than a single
  linear scan of all keys.
* `ScanSchemeDecoding.scan_maximum` — `triangle N` is the greatest achievable cost.
* `ScanSchemeDecoding.scan_cost_spectrum` — every scan scheme on `N` keys with `m > 0`
  buckets has total cost in the closed interval `[triangleOpt N m, triangle N]`, and both
  endpoints are realised.
-/

namespace ScanSchemeDecoding

open Finset

/-- **Superadditivity** of the triangular cost: merging two buckets never helps. -/
theorem triangle_add_le (a b : ℕ) : triangle a + triangle b ≤ triangle (a + b) := by
  have ha := two_mul_triangle a
  have hb := two_mul_triangle b
  have hab := two_mul_triangle (a + b)
  nlinarith [Nat.zero_le (a * b)]

/-- Splitting keys into buckets never costs more than one linear scan of everything. -/
theorem sum_triangle_le {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → ℕ) :
    ∑ i ∈ s, triangle (f i) ≤ triangle (∑ i ∈ s, f i) := by
  classical
  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp

# Triangular cost and the exact `ε`-pigeonhole optimum

This file develops the arithmetic backbone of the *scan-scheme* cost model.

A scan scheme distributes `N` keys into `m` buckets; decoding a key costs its
`1`-based position inside its bucket, so a bucket holding `k` keys contributes
`1 + 2 + ⋯ + k = triangle k` to the total decoding cost.  Optimising a scheme is
therefore exactly the discrete problem

  minimise `∑ i, triangle (f i)`  subject to `f : Fin m → ℕ`, `∑ i, f i = N`.

## Main results

* `ScanSchemeDecoding.triangle_tangent` — the *integral tangent-line inequality*
  `triangle q + (q+1) * (k - q) ≤ triangle k`, valid for **all** naturals `k, q`
  (over `ℤ`), the discrete convexity fact driving everything below.
* `ScanSchemeDecoding.sum_triangle_ge` — the exact pigeonhole lower bound
  `r * triangle (q+1) + (m - r) * triangle q ≤ ∑ i, triangle (f i)` where
  `q = N / m`, `r = N % m`.
* `ScanSchemeDecoding.sum_triangle_balanced` — the balanced profile attains it,
  so the bound is the *exact* optimum, not merely a bound.
* `ScanSchemeDecoding.triangleOpt_two_mul_ge` — the averaged ("`ε`") form:

open Finset

/-- `triangle k = 1 + 2 + ⋯ + k`, the cost of scanning a bucket of size `k`
when every key of the bucket is decoded once. -/
def triangle (k : ℕ) : ℕ := k * (k + 1) / 2

@[simp] lemma triangle_zero : triangle 0 = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma triangle_one : triangle 1 = 1 := rfl

lemma two_mul_triangle (k : ℕ) : 2 * triangle k = k * (k + 1) := by
  have h : 2 ∣ k * (k + 1) := (Nat.even_mul_succ_self k).two_dvd
  rw [triangle, Nat.mul_div_cancel' h]

lemma triangle_succ (k : ℕ) : triangle (k + 1) = triangle k + (k + 1) := by
  have h1 := two_mul_triangle k
  have h2 := two_mul_triangle (k + 1)
  have h3 : (k + 1) * (k + 1 + 1) = k * (k + 1) + 2 * (k + 1) := by ring
  omega

/-- `triangle` as a sum: the cost of decoding every key of a bucket of size `k`. -/
lemma triangle_eq_sum (k : ℕ) : triangle k = ∑ j ∈ range k, (j + 1) := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih => rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ← ih, triangle_succ]

/-- **Integral tangent-line inequality.**  Discrete convexity of `triangle` at the

  have hr : r < m := Nat.mod_lt _ hm
  obtain ⟨s, hs⟩ : ∃ s, m = s + r := ⟨m - r, by omega⟩
  have hmr : m - r = s := by omega
  unfold triangleOpt
  rw [triangle_succ, ← hq, ← hrdef, hmr]
  have h1 := two_mul_triangle q
  have hNsub : N = (s + r) * q + r := by rw [← hN, hs]
  calc N * (q + 1) = ((s + r) * q + r) * (q + 1) := by rw [← hNsub]
    _ ≤ (r + s) * (q * (q + 1)) + 2 * r * (q + 1) := by nlinarith [Nat.zero_le (r * (q+1))]
    _ = 2 * (r * (triangle q + (q + 1)) + s * triangle q) := by rw [← h1]; ring

  "future_directions": "# Future Directions — scan schemes after the exact optimum

The cycle just closed established, with complete proofs:

* honest uniqueness decoding through an explicitly constructed **intra-bucket index**:
  the pair (bucket label, intra-bucket index) decodes back to its key, and is the only
  pair that does;
* **exact cost accounting**: total decoding cost equals the sum over buckets of the
  triangular number of the bucket size, identically;
* the exact `ε`-pigeonhole optimum `Opt(N,m) = r·T(q+1) + (m−r)·T(q)`, *attained* by the
  residue scheme `x ↦ x mod m`;
* **rigidity** of that optimum: a scheme is cost-optimal precisely when every bucket
  holds `⌊N/m⌋` or `⌈N/m⌉` keys;
* the `ε`-compression barrier `1/(2ε)` with matching equality case, achieved by the
  residue scheme whenever `m` divides `N`;
* the cost window `[Opt(N,m), T(N)]`, with both endpoints realised.

What follows are the next bold, falsifiable steps. Each is stated so that a single
theorem would confirm or refute it.

## Conjecture 1 (Enumerative rigidity: an exact formula for the optimal locus)

The number of cost-optimal bucket maps from `N` keys to `m` buckets is exactly

  `C(m, r) · N! / ((q+1)!^r · (q!)^(m−r))`,  with `q = ⌊N/m⌋`, `r = N mod m`,

i.e. `#{S : cost(S) = Opt(N,m)} = C(m, r) · multinomial(N; q+1 repeated r times, q
repeated m−r times)`. Verified by exhaustive enumeration for `(N,m) = (5,3)`
(`3 · 30 = 90`), `(6,3)` (`90`), `(7,3)` (`630`), `(7,4)` (`2520`) and `(8,3)` (`1680`).

*The key insight is* that rigidity turns an optimisation problem into an exact
combinatorial description of the optimal locus, so counting optimal schemes becomes a
pure multinomial count; and the `Sym(keys) × Sym(buckets)` invariance already proved
says the locus is a single group orbit — the formula is then the orbit–stabiliser
theorem.

*Why now?* Both ingredients — the characterisation of the optimal locus as exactly the
balanced profiles, and the invariance of the cost under relabelling keys and buckets —
are established; only the multinomial-counting step needs to be supplied.

## Problem 2 (The structure of the achievable cost set)

*Status: the original form of this conjecture — that the achievable costs fill the whole
integer interval `[Opt(N,m), T(N)]` — is refuted by exhaustive enumeration.* For
`(N,m) = (5,3)` the achievable totals are `{7, 8, 9, 11, 15}`, so `10, 12, 13, 14` are
not achievable although they lie in the window `[7,15]`; for `(6,3)` the achievable set
is `{9,10,12,13,16,21}`, and for `(7,3)` it is `{12,13,14,16,17,18,22,28}`.

The correct statement is that the achievable set is exactly

  `{ Σ_i T(k_i) : (k_i) a partition of N into at most m parts }`,

which follows from exact cost accounting together with the symmetry invariance. The
refined open problem is to describe the gap structure explicitly. Moving a single key
from a bucket of size `a` to one of size `b` changes the total cost by exactly
`b + 1 − a`, so the achievable set is the orbit of the balanced profile under these unit
moves; a plausible precise statement is that it is *gapless on an initial segment*
`[Opt(N,m), B(N,m)]` for an explicit threshold `B(N,m)`, and sparse above it.

## Conjecture 3 (Two-level scan schemes and the `1/(2ε)` barrier)

Iterating the construction — a bucket map into `m₁` buckets followed by a second bucket
map into `m₂` sub-buckets inside each bucket — cannot beat the one-level barrier at
equal total space: for every two-level scheme with `m₁ · m₂ ≤ ε · N` sub-buckets, the
mean decoding cost is at least `1/(2ε)`.

*The key insight is* that exact cost accounting applies verbatim at each level: the cost
of the refined structure is again a sum of triangular numbers over the finest fibres,
whose number is bounded by `m₁ · m₂`. Establishing this would show that hierarchy does
not evade the space–time product, and that the constant `1/2` is a property of scanning
itself rather than of any particular table layout.

## Problem 4 (Weighted keys)

Replace the uniform access distribution by weights `w(x) ≥ 0` and minimise
`Σ_x w(x) · cost(x)`. Within a bucket the optimal scan order is by decreasing weight (an
exchange argument), so the problem becomes a weighted partition problem; the convexity
mechanism above should be replaced by a majorisation argument, and it is unclear whether
an exact closed-form optimum survives.

## Problem 5 (Beyond linear scan)

Replace the intra-bucket linear scan by binary search, so that a bucket of size `k` costs
`Σ_{j<k} (1 + ⌊log₂ j⌋)`. This cost function is still convex but no longer polynomial;
the tangent-line method should still yield an exact optimum with a modified balanced
profile, and the corresponding barrier would be expected to degrade from `1/(2ε)` to
`Θ(log(1/ε))`.
",
  "modules": {
    "demo": """"
Scan schemes: honest uniqueness decoding, exact cost accounting,
the pigeonhole optimum, rigidity, and the 1/(2*eps) compression barrier.

Everything in this file is self-contained (standard library only) and mirrors,
numerically, the theorems of the accompanying paper:

  * triangle(k) = k(k+1)/2 is the cost of scanning every key of a bucket of size k;
  * total cost of a scheme = sum over buckets of triangle(bucket size)  (exact);
  * min over all schemes = triangleOpt(N, m)
        = r * triangle(q+1) + (m-r) * triangle(q),   q = N // m, r = N % m;
  * the residue scheme x |-> x mod m attains it;
  * a scheme is optimal iff every bucket has size q or q+1 (rigidity);
  * max over all schemes = triangle(N), attained by the one-bucket scheme;
  * mean cost >= (N/m + 1)/2, hence >= 1/(2*eps) whenever m <= eps*N.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Dict, Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Triangular cost and the exact optimum
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def triangle(k: int) -> int:
    """triangle(k) = 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2, the cost of scanning a bucket of size k."""
    return k * (k + 1) // 2


def triangle_opt(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """The exact minimal total decoding cost of n keys in m buckets."""
    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("m must be positive")
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return r * triangle(q + 1) + (m - r) * triangle(q)


def balanced_profile(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The balanced bucket-size profile: r buckets of size q+1, m-r of size q."""
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    return [q + 1 if i < r else q for i in range(m)]


def tangent_slack(k: int, q: int) -> int:
    """triangle(k) - [triangle(q) + (q+1)(k-q)] = (k-q)(k-q-1)/2 >= 0."""
    d = k - q
    return d * (d - 1) // 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Scan schemes: encoding, decoding, exact cost
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class ScanScheme:
    """A scan scheme on keys 0..n-1 with m buckets, given by a bucket map."""

    def __init__(self, n: int, m: int, bucket_map: Sequence[int]) -> None:
        if len(bucket_map) != n:
            raise ValueError("bucket_map must have one entry per key")
        if any(not (0 <= b < m) for b in bucket_map):
            raise ValueError("bucket labels out of range")
        self.n: int = n
        self.m: int = m
        self.bucket: List[int] = list(bucket_map)

    def fiber(self, b: int) -> List[int]:
        """The keys stored in bucket b, in the order in which a scan visits them."""
        return [x for x in range(self.n) if self.bucket[x] == b]

    def scan_list(self, b: int) -> List[int]:
        """Alias for the fiber, emphasising that it is an ordered scan sequence."""
        return self.fiber(b)

    def idx(self, x: int) -> int:
        """The intra-bucket index of key x: its 0-based position in its own bucket."""
        return self.scan_list(self.bucket[x]).index(x)

    def decode_cost(self, x: int) -> int:
        """1-based number of comparisons a scan performs to find x."""
        return self.idx(x) + 1

    def encode(self, x: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
        """The scan code of x: (bucket label, intra-bucket index)."""
        return (self.bucket[x], self.idx(x))

    def decode(self, code: Tuple[int, int]) -> int | None:
        """Read off the entry at the given index of the given bucket, if any."""
        b, i = code
        lst = self.scan_list(b)
        return lst[i] if 0 <= i < len(lst) else None

    def profile(self) -> List[int]:
        """The bucket-size profile of the scheme."""
        return [len(self.fiber(b)) for b in range(self.m)]

    def total_cost(self) -> int:
        """Total decoding cost, summed over all keys."""
        return sum(self.decode_cost(x) for x in range(self.n))

    def mean_cost(self) -> float:
        return self.total_cost() / self.n if self.n else 0.0


def mod_scheme(n: int, m: int) -> ScanScheme:
    """The residue scheme: key x is stored in bucket x mod m."""
    return ScanScheme(n, m, [x % m for x in range(n)])


def const_scheme(n: int, m: int) -> ScanScheme:
    """The degenerate scheme: every key in bucket 0."""
    return ScanScheme(n, m, [0] * n)


def all_schemes(n: int, m: int) -> Iterator[ScanScheme]:
    """Enumerate all m^n scan schemes (only for tiny n, m)."""
    for bm in product(range(m), repeat=n):
        yield ScanScheme(n, m, bm)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Checks corresponding to the theorems
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_honest_decoding(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    """decode(encode(x)) = x, and (b,i) decodes to x iff (b,i) = encode(x)."""
    for x in range(scheme.n):
        if scheme.decode(scheme.encode(x)) != x:
            return False
    for b in range(scheme.m):
        for i in range(scheme.n + 1):
            y = scheme.decode((b, i))
            if y is not None and (b, i) != scheme.encode(y):
                return False
    return True


def check_cost_accounting(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    """Total cost equals the sum of triangular numbers of the bucket sizes."""
    return scheme.total_cost() == sum(triangle(k) for k in scheme.profile())


def is_balanced(scheme: ScanScheme) -> bool:
    q = scheme.n // scheme.m
    return all(q <= k <= q + 1 for k in scheme.profile())


def brute_force_extremes(n: int, m: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    costs = [s.total_cost() for s in all_schemes(n, m)]
    return min(costs), max(costs)


def achievable_costs(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    return sorted({s.total_cost() for s in all_schemes(n, m)})


def partitions_into_at_most(n: int, m: int, cap: int | None = None) -> Iterator[List[int]]:
    """All multisets of at most m positive parts summing to n, in weakly decreasing order."""
    if cap is None:
        cap = n
    if n == 0:
        yield []
        return
    if m == 0:
        return
    for part in range(min(n, cap), 0, -1):
        for rest in partitions_into_at_most(n - part, m - 1, part):
            yield [part] + rest


def partition_costs(n: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The predicted achievable cost set: sums of triangular numbers over size profiles."""
    return sorted({sum(triangle(k) for k in p) for p in partitions_into_at_most(n, m)})


def count_optimal_schemes(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    opt = triangle_opt(n, m)
    return sum(1 for s in all_schemes(n, m) if s.total_cost() == opt)


def predicted_optimal_count(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """C(m, r) * multinomial(n; q+1 repeated r times, q repeated m-r times)."""
    q, r = divmod(n, m)
    multinomial = factorial(n) // (factorial(q + 1) ** r * factorial(q) ** (m - r))
    return comb(m, r) * multinomial


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Reporting
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def section(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 72)


def demo_honest_decoding() -> None:
    section("1. Honest uniqueness decoding and exact cost accounting")
    n, m = 12, 5
    s = mod_scheme(n, m)
    print(f"keys N = {n}, buckets m = {m}, scheme: x -> x mod {m}")
    print("bucket profile:", s.profile())
    print()
    print(" key | bucket | index | code    | decode(code) | cost")
    print("-----+--------+-------+---------+--------------+-----")
    for x in range(n):
        b, i = s.encode(x)
        print(f" {x:3d} | {b:6d} | {i:5d} | ({b},{i})   | {s.decode((b, i)):12d} | {s.decode_cost(x):4d}")
    print()
    print("every code decodes back to its own key, uniquely:", check_honest_decoding(s))
    print("total cost              :", s.total_cost())
    print("sum of triangle(sizes)  :", sum(triangle(k) for k in s.profile()))
    print("exact accounting holds  :", check_cost_accounting(s))


def demo_optimum() -> None:
    section("2. The exact pigeonhole optimum, verified by brute force")
    print(" N   m | triangleOpt | brute-force min | triangle(N) | brute-force max")
    print("-------+-------------+-----------------+-------------+----------------")
    for n, m in [(4, 2), (5, 3), (6, 3), (7, 3), (6, 4), (8, 3)]:
        lo, hi = brute_force_extremes(n, m)
        print(f"{n:3d} {m:3d} | {triangle_opt(n, m):11d} | {lo:15d} | {triangle(n):11d} | {hi:15d}")
    print()
    print("The residue scheme attains the optimum on the nose:")
    for n, m in [(10, 3), (17, 5), (100, 7), (1000, 32)]:
        s = mod_scheme(n, m)
        print(f"  N={n:5d} m={m:3d}: cost {s.total_cost():7d} = triangleOpt {triangle_opt(n, m):7d}"
              f"  ({s.total_cost() == triangle_opt(n, m)})")


def demo_tangent() -> None:
    section("3. Where the lower bound comes from: the integral tangent line")
    q = 4
    print(f"tangent to triangle at q = {q}:  triangle(q) + (q+1)(k-q) = {triangle(q)} + {q+1}(k-{q})")
    print()
    print("  k | triangle(k) | tangent value | slack (k-q)(k-q-1)/2")
    print("----+-------------+---------------+---------------------")
    for k in range(0, 10):
        tangent = triangle(q) + (q + 1) * (k - q)
        print(f" {k:2d} | {triangle(k):11d} | {tangent:13d} | {tangent_slack(k, q):19d}")
    print()
    print("slack vanishes exactly at k = q and k = q+1 -- this is the source of rigidity.")


def demo_rigidity() -> None:
    section("4. Rigidity: the optimal schemes are exactly the balanced ones")
    for n, m in [(5, 3), (6, 3), (7, 4)]:
        opt = triangle_opt(n, m)
        agree = all((s.total_cost() == opt) == is_balanced(s) for s in all_schemes(n, m))
        cnt = count_optimal_schemes(n, m)
        pred = predicted_optimal_count(n, m)
        print(f"N={n} m={m}: optimum {opt};  'optimal <=> balanced' holds: {agree};"
              f"  #optimal = {cnt}, formula C(m,r)*multinomial = {pred}"
              f"  ({'match' if cnt == pred else 'MISMATCH'})")
    print()
    print("(The counting formula is a conjecture; here it is confirmed by exhaustive search.)")


def demo_spectrum() -> None:
    section("5. The cost spectrum: every scheme lies in [triangleOpt(N,m), triangle(N)]")
    print("The window is correct and both endpoints are attained; but the achievable")
    print("set inside the window is NOT the full integer interval -- it is exactly the")
    print("set of sums of triangular numbers over partitions of N into at most m parts.")
    print()
    for n, m in [(5, 3), (6, 3), (6, 2), (7, 3)]:
        costs = achievable_costs(n, m)
        lo, hi = triangle_opt(n, m), triangle(n)
        inside = costs[0] == lo and costs[-1] == hi
        print(f"N={n} m={m}: achievable costs {costs}")
        print(f"          window [{lo}, {hi}] with both endpoints attained: {inside}")
        print(f"          gapless: {costs == list(range(lo, hi + 1))};"
              f"  equals partition prediction: {costs == partition_costs(n, m)}")


def demo_perfect_hashing() -> None:
    section("6. Perfect hashing and the failure analysis")
    n, m = 6, 6
    s = ScanScheme(n, m, list(range(n)))
    print(f"N={n}, m={m}, identity bucket map: all costs = 1?",
          all(s.decode_cost(x) == 1 for x in range(n)))
    print("bucket map injective?", len(set(s.bucket)) == n)
    print()
    n, m = 6, 4
    s = mod_scheme(n, m)
    print(f"N={n} > m={m}: some key must cost at least 2 ->",
          max(s.decode_cost(x) for x in range(n)) >= 2)
    print("a key whose cost is at least N/m (rounded up):")
    for x in range(n):
        if m * s.decode_cost(x) >= n:
            print(f"  key {x}: m * cost = {m * s.decode_cost(x)} >= N = {n}")
            break


def demo_epsilon_barrier() -> None:
    section("7. The 1/(2*eps) compression barrier")
    n = 4096
    print(f"N = {n} keys.  m <= eps*N buckets forces mean cost >= 1/(2*eps).")
    print()
    print("   eps |    m | 1/(2eps) | (N/m+1)/2 | residue-scheme mean cost")
    print("-------+------+----------+-----------+-------------------------")
    for eps in [1 / 2, 1 / 4, 1 / 8, 1 / 16, 1 / 32, 1 / 64]:
        m = int(eps * n)
        s = mod_scheme(n, m)
        print(f" {eps:6.4f} | {m:4d} | {1/(2*eps):8.3f} | {(n/m + 1)/2:9.3f} | {s.mean_cost():23.3f}")
    print()
    print("When m divides N the residue scheme meets the bound exactly:")
    for m in [2, 4, 8, 16]:
        s = mod_scheme(n, m)
        lhs = 2 * m * s.total_cost()
        rhs = n * (n + m)
        print(f"  m={m:3d}: 2*m*cost = {lhs} , N*(N+m) = {rhs}  ({lhs == rhs})")


def demo_symmetry() -> None:
    section("8. The cost depends only on the bucket-size partition")
    n, m = 8, 3
    base = ScanScheme(n, m, [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2])
    perm = [3, 1, 7, 0, 5, 2, 6, 4]  # a permutation of the keys
    relabel = {0: 2, 1: 0, 2: 1}  # a permutation of the bucket labels
    permuted = ScanScheme(n, m, [base.bucket[perm[x]] for x in range(n)])
    relabelled = ScanScheme(n, m, [relabel[b] for b in base.bucket])
    print("base profile      :", base.profile(), "cost", base.total_cost())
    print("key-permuted      :", permuted.profile(), "cost", permuted.total_cost())
    print("bucket-relabelled :", relabelled.profile(), "cost", relabelled.total_cost())
    print("all three equal   :",
          base.total_cost() == permuted.total_cost() == relabelled.total_cost())


def main() -> None:
    print("Scan schemes: honest decoding, exact costs, and the compression barrier")
    demo_honest_decoding()
    demo_optimum()
    demo_tangent()
    demo_rigidity()
    demo_spectrum()
    demo_perfect_hashing()
    demo_epsilon_barrier()
    demo_symmetry()
    print()
    print("All numerical checks completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
